mfrmr roadmap

Source: ROADMAP.md

mfrmr connects three tasks in performance assessment:

  1. Measurement models: estimate person ability while accounting for rater severity, task or criterion difficulty, category thresholds, and supported discrimination or dependence structures.
  2. G-theory assessment planning: separate observed-score variance components in a G-Study and project reliability, generalizability (G), dependability (Phi), and standard errors across candidate rating designs in a D-Study.
  3. Rater feedback and decision support: turn agreement, fit, residual, network, bias/DFF, and conditional classification analyses into structured, reviewable evidence without automating high-stakes rater exclusion or causal fairness claims.

The goal is a reproducible route from a rating design to defensible scores, feedback and future assessment plans. The package remains a single package, with optional external tools for specialized estimation and secondary analysis. This roadmap distinguishes implemented development features, release conditions and research candidates. For changes already implemented in 0.3.0, see NEWS and help("mfrmr_api_migration_030").

Users can choose measurement, planning and feedback independently. Dataset-specific preparation and downstream survey analysis can use separate scripts or optional articles; they need not share one mfrmr entry point.

The core analysis entries are fit_mfrm(), diagnose_mfrm(), mfrm_g_study() and mfrm_d_study(). Keep their input roles, result-object meanings and supported summary(), plot() and confint() workflows stable within the 0.3 series. describe_mfrm_data() reviews inputs; mfrm_results() and mfrm_report() organize supported results. The default mfrmr_output_guide() connects these routes; specialist tools remain available through an explicit scope. Model-specific support and uncertainty restrictions still apply.

From a native fit, mfrm_report(fit, type = ...) selects specification, data quality, category, facet-statistics, precision, checklist and reference review components. Saved bias estimates also support interaction, recalibration history and pairwise reports; saved DFF analyses support narrative reports. Optimization replay remains a distinct report type. Collected results continue to use mfrm_report(res) with their supported styles and formats.

What should become easier in 0.3.0?

The intended benefit is a connected assessment workflow: start with a rating table, understand the design and diagnostics, and use the results to prepare feedback or compare a future rating plan. The development tour source connects this sequence with data, figures, explanations and a saved analysis. The release work includes checking the complete example and its corresponding website version; a working section alone does not establish the whole workflow. The ICNALE essay-rating example extends that sequence to a licensed external workbook obtained by the reader. It keeps fixed CAF dimensions distinct from sampled tasks and separates latent-scale calibration from observed-score planning. The repository provides the workflow code without distributing corpus data or individual results.

Your question The workflow should help you do this
Can I compare people rated by different panels? Inspect who rated whom, distinguish missing assignments from zero scores, and review model identification. A connected graph alone is insufficient.
What should I discuss with a rater? Read severity together with consistency, exposure and uncertainty; prepare a reviewable report without automatic rater exclusion.
Should I add raters or tasks? Compare precision with total ratings, rater workload and resource limits. Known calibrated panels use conditional information; sampled future rater/task populations use the separate observed-score G/Phi route. Neither supplies an automatic optimum.
Can I reproduce this result later? Save the analysis, diagnostics and numerical plot data together, and reload them for reporting.

TAM, mirt, sirt or FACETS can remain the right choice for a particular model or established workflow. Their capabilities already include flexible latent models, information curves and, in applicable packages, rater facets and discrimination. mfrmr’s aim is to connect rating assignments, interpretable estimates, assessment planning and reviewable rater feedback through reusable results. This is a workflow goal, not a claim of a new information formula or superior estimation. Beginner comprehension and successful use still need evaluation.

Milestones and dependencies

“Implemented” means available in development source within a documented scope. It does not mean released, or validated for every rating design. The sequence below describes outcomes and completion conditions rather than calendar promises. Existing numerical and saved-result evidence remains useful when the relevant code, inputs and settings have not changed.

Stage What users should be able to do Remaining completion condition
0.2.4.1 — repair the published 0.2.4 Use corrected diagnostics, boundary reporting and figures through the existing interface Validate the repair-only distribution, including BLAS-portable tests, mice compatibility and applicable existing-feature fixes. Evaluate Windows results and total check time before publication.
0.3.0 — interpret estimates and uncertainty Identify the estimate, its scale, whether an interval is available, and the reason for a limitation Reconcile final outputs, help and saved results for the supported model/estimator combinations. Retain valid point estimates when only the interval is unavailable. Distinguish finite estimates, limiting fits, unidentified quantities and numerical failure.
0.3.0 — compare rating plans Compare additional raters, tasks or assignments against precision and operational burden Complete the two planning routes below, preserving every declared candidate, assumptions, missing costs and inconclusive comparisons through plots and saved reports.
0.3.0 — prepare rater feedback Trace a diagnostic flag to the relevant ratings and decide what warrants substantive review Connect severity, consistency, exposure, missingness and uncertainty without automatic rater exclusion. Verify that unavailable diagnostics remain distinguishable from reassuring results.
0.3.0 — navigate and reproduce an analysis Start from a short help example, find specialist conditions, customize a figure, and reload results Align migration examples, supported saved objects, numerical plot data and reports. Check the complete affected example and website interactions; keep essential interpretation available offline.
0.3.0 — release a consistent package and website Follow documentation that matches the installed version Once the preceding scope is settled, validate the final archive in the required environments, evaluate check duration and remaining issues, and verify the matching website and distribution.
0.3.x — selected extensions and stronger guidance Use additional explanatory or linked models, specify selected step constraints, or make better-supported design recommendations Select a concrete missing capability or recommendation. Establish its target, identifiable design and required evidence before adding it. These are separate adoption decisions, not one required bundle.
0.4.x and later — selected new model families Answer a question that the existing models or an external workflow cannot adequately address Select a model branch, then establish identification, independent numerical checks, computational feasibility and evidence for its intended interpretation.

Maintenance corrections come first and do not wait for a new model, a redesigned interface or a general sample-size guideline. The 0.3.0 estimation conditions define the scope of planning and feedback; documentation and saved-result work can proceed alongside them. Final packaging follows integration of that scope. An error in supported functionality must be corrected. A broader claim that lacks evidence remains explicitly limited or moves to later research.

The immediate design priority is precision versus burden. Keep these routes separate:

Rating decision Existing route What the comparison can support
Add or reassign known calibrated rater/task levels for one Person’s plan compute_information(rating_plan = ...), plot() and plot_data() Conditional information over a declared ability range, with rating counts and workload assumptions. This does not include calibration uncertainty or predict an uncalibrated rater.
Change the number of raters/tasks sampled from a declared future population G-Study, supported D-Study comparisons and recommend_mfrm_design() Observed-score G/Phi/SEM, resource limits and supported paired differences. Increasing future counts does not add information to the original G-Study.

In either workflow, retain all proposed plans, unavailable precision and unknown costs. Total cohort workload and each rater’s workload are different quantities. Adding raters does not by itself redistribute existing assignments. Neither route establishes an automatic optimum or a universal minimum sample size. The development visual tour connects the calculation, interpretation and saving steps.

Later research starts from a decision that current evidence cannot support:

  • Design guidance: use the existing small studies to select informative conditions, then confirm the proposed recommendation independently. Distinguish Persons, raters, tasks, overlap and ratings per Person; retain failures and Monte Carlo uncertainty. If the evidence is insufficient, provide conditional guidance rather than a universal rule.
  • Explanatory and linked models: identify the owner of each covariate, scale constraint and uncertainty target before extending estimation. Extensions to Person latent regression, rater-experience models, linking uncertainty and mixed category sets require separate decisions.
  • New model families: select one branch for a concrete need. An existing external-software route may be sufficient; model-name count is not a goal.

Formative evaluation can use the current estimation, planning and feedback workflows without waiting for another model. Observe whether intended readers can find the relevant result, explain its limits and complete the task. Until that is evaluated, shorter help and successful examples are editorial and technical improvements, not demonstrated gains in comprehension. Dataset tutorials, including IEA and survey-analysis recipes, remain optional applications with no assigned package-release milestone.

Starting from the published 0.2.4 release

CRAN published 0.2.4 on 2026-10-30. It is the stable reference for this roadmap; 0.2.4.9000 is development toward 0.3.0, not a replacement already available from CRAN.

Repair-only release 0.2.4.1 is being prepared from published 0.2.4 before the 0.3.0 interface transition. It addresses BLAS-portable tests, mice compatibility and verified existing-feature defects while retaining public entry points, numerical engines and supported saved-model meanings. Corrections to availability or reporting state their conditions and effects in NEWS. The GitHub 0.2.5 maintenance snapshot remains separate. New model options, interval procedures and interface redesigns remain in the development series.

For figures, 0.2.4.1 retains base graphics and optional as_ggplot() conversion. Maintenance corrections reject conflicting Person group labels, align group-density exclusions with the main Wright map, and distinguish group names from facet legend entries. Invalid group specifications are rejected; groups too small for a density curve are omitted with an explanation when no curve can be drawn. These corrections do not require the new ggplot return contract or a change to the default visual theme.

Area Published 0.2.4 Intended change in 0.3.0
Public entry points 189 exports 156 exports: consolidate 35 names into shared routes and add facets_guide() / import_irt_fit(). Follow the migration guide for exact replacements.
Two-family GPCM Experimental two-facet MML Choose two slope facets among fixed additive facets, with separate step ownership and a named slope reference; retain experimental inference limits.
Model specification Flat fit_mfrm() arguments Group advanced model choices in spec and numerical settings in control, with validated legacy calls.
Figures and saved results Base graphics, saved plot payloads and optional as_ggplot() conversion Return editable ggplot objects consistently, with a restrained shared theme; use plot_data() for numerical payloads. Preserve supported saved-result classes and methods.
Bayesian workflows Export and posterior-summary review Direct data/spec export, optional CmdStanR execution, joint-draw contrasts and new-Person scoring with separate predictive-precision checks.
Assessment planning G-Study / D-Study and paired contrasts Review a declared finite set of plans against costs, limits and targets, preserving pointwise uncertainty and avoiding an automatic optimum claim.
Learning and reference Extensive reference help and tutorials A visual entry page, five core offline tutorials, specialist website articles and shorter task-focused reference navigation.

Reliability plots and compute_information() already exist in 0.2.4; they are not new statistical capabilities in 0.3.0. Improve their visibility and interpretation: distinguish Person/rater separation, observed agreement, G/Phi and ability-dependent information. By default, the information total uses all observed rating exposures. In 0.3.0, compute_information(rating_plan = ...) also evaluates a declared plan for one Person using fitted facet levels and independent rating counts. It supports converged additive MML RSM, PCM and one-family GPCM calibrations within its documented boundary restrictions. Plans retain their assignments, counts and fixed-calibration interpretation when plotted or saved. GPCM comparisons using working coordinates without primary slope estimates remain explicitly exploratory. This comparison does not propagate calibration uncertainty, predict an uncalibrated rater, supply EAP uncertainty or choose an optimal allocation. G/Phi comparisons remain a separate observed-score analysis.

0.3.0: migration and release conditions

The capabilities in the comparison table are implemented in the development source. They are not yet a CRAN release. The next interface-changing release is 0.3.0 because consolidating public names and changing plot() returns require script updates:

  • Replace retired entry points using the help("mfrmr_api_migration_030").
  • Extract plotted numerical values with plot_data(); plot() returns a ggplot object. Supported saved 0.2.x result classes and legacy plot payloads retain their documented methods.
  • Use complete argument names with fit_mfrm() and do.call(). Only the first four positional arguments retain their old positions. Abbreviations for names now passed through ... are not supported; the migration guide gives before/after calls.

The 0.3.0 default figures use a white background, restrained grids and spacing suited to papers, presentations and screen reading. Existing presets provide the initial appearance; ordinary ggplot edits control finer details. Save the edited ggplot to retain those edits: plot_data() contains the original statistical payload and settings. Explicitly sized text layers may need their own adjustments. Representative exports and saved-object checks support this design; they do not establish readability at every size or improved user comprehension.

Wright-map group displays in 0.3.0 additionally provide a shared adjustable bandwidth, Person-level rug marks, empirical CDF values and exclusion counts. They describe fitted Person estimates, not a latent population density or a DIF/DFF test. These display extensions are separate from the maintenance fixes.

Interface changes and faster numerical kernels retain the documented statistical targets, quadrature rules, convergence criteria and independent checks. They do not establish finite-sample inference validity for additional models or rating designs. Shared spec lists remain subject to each function’s scope, including the export limits below.

Alternative response equations and later model candidates below are outside 0.3.0; supported-scope errors and misleading claims still require correction.

Measurement models: current limits and extension order

Model choice and estimation method are separate decisions. Current native support in 0.2.4.9000 is bounded as follows; consult help("mfrmr_gpcm_scope") and help("fit_mfrm_technical_details") for the complete conditions.

Response model Native estimation paths Boundary that extensions must preserve
Ordinary RSM / PCM MML, ordinary JML and CML within their documented scopes; a separate Jeffreys-penalized JML path Fixed versus estimated ability populations change the MML model. Numerical admissibility alone does not validate small-sample intervals.
One-family GPCM, shared step and slope facet MML, ordinary JML and experimental profile-score-adjusted JML The adjustment is not a general small-sample correction for every model; its root-variation SE does not establish structural-parameter interval coverage.
One-family GPCM, separate step and slope facets MML JML and its profile-score adjustment are not supported for this specification.
Two-family GPCM Experimental fixed-grid EM or adaptive-direct MML Two named slope facets among the declared fixed additive facets; step ownership, the noncentered location facet and the geometric-mean-one slope reference are separately specified. Ability remains fixed to N(0,1).

With few informative ratings per Person, ordinary JML can retain incidental-parameter bias even as the number of Persons increases. The number of categories or fitted steps alone does not determine that bias. mfrmr does not apply a universal test-length multiplier. RSM/PCM CML, population-based MML, Jeffreys-penalized JML and the restricted GPCM profile-score adjustment have different assumptions and uncertainty targets; none is a blanket guarantee of bias removal. The stability guide will evaluate exposure and category use separately from Person count, including residual bias and failed estimates.

The two-family GPCM implementation retains the current response equation, in which both slope factors multiply the whole ability-minus-location-and-step expression. For example, Task and Rater can own slopes while Criterion owns steps. Use slope_reference to name the slope family with geometric mean one and noncenter_facet to name the sole uncentered location facet. Additional Occasion or Venue effects remain fixed additive effects, not extra ability dimensions. The old two-facet defaults and saved fits retain their meaning. Extended portable calibrations use format 7; the original two-facet structure retains format 6.

Three- and five-facet calculations and representative workflows are checked. These checks do not guarantee identification, convergence or interval coverage for every design. In particular, an optimizer can converge while the integration checks refuse intervals or portable scoring. Extended-role Stan export from an existing fit supports posterior reload, contrasts, plots and reports. Two-family simulation, direct data/spec export and new-Person posterior scoring remain unsupported. Changing the slope reference with fresh independent priors changes the Bayesian model. This extension is included in 0.3.0. Its point-estimation review separates identification, numerical accuracy and sampling error; adding support does not remove experimental interval restrictions. Point estimates now carry separate numerical and boundary status in summaries and reports. A converged value at a chosen integration rule is distinguished from a solution with automatic integration and score checks; neither is a guarantee of a unique global maximum or adequate small-sample accuracy.

For supported all-low/all-high boundary cases, the remaining targets can be estimated through a separate limiting-likelihood fit, including models with rater-owned steps or a criterion without slopes. One affected facet outside the reference slope family can be reduced when at least two of its levels and all other facet levels remain. Unidentified slopes or free steps of removed levels are distinguished from remaining estimates and binary steps fixed at zero. These point estimates do not qualify ordinary full-model intervals. For ordinary finite fits, experimental step-offset intervals use confint(fit, parm = "steps"), with the full joint covariance and within-level sum-zero constraints. They retain numerical checks and unqualified coverage; binary steps fixed at zero have no inferential interval.

Per-level rating-design tables separate distinct persons, rating rows, per-person exposure, marginal facet crossings and category use. Full-model and limiting-fit counts are labelled separately. These descriptions help inspect the data behind each estimate; they are not sample-size guarantees.

A bounded three-facet study now separates Person count from ratings per Person. All numerical checks passed, but the 60-Person, four-rating Task-slope interval covered its true value in 183/200 replications. The design, Monte Carlo uncertainty and precision results are described in the development GPCM guide. They do not establish a general minimum sample size or remove experimental interval restrictions. The number of levels of each facet was fixed at two.

Point-estimation checks address identification, starting values, integration, curvature and sampling error separately. A positive local Hessian is not proof of a unique global maximum. Supported point estimates remain usable when the corresponding interval is unqualified or unavailable. Extension decisions must preserve this distinction throughout prediction, reporting and saved results.

Two-family JML, its bias correction, alternative slope placement and the Uto (2021) response equation are separate candidates. They require their own identification and estimation contracts. A Bayesian implementation must specify the link coefficient, ability scale and constrained prior density; reproducing the published appendix and adopting a different symmetric prior are distinct choices. A logistic link with coefficient 1.7 is not an exact normal-ogive link. Metric conversion must preserve probabilities and transform covariance and priors consistently.

These candidates are considered alongside ordinary-model needs: mixed binary and polytomous category sets, rubric differences, and uncertainty in linked calibrations. Current native fits use one declared category range; a step facet does not provide facet-specific category support. The choice to extend mfrmr or use a supported TAM/ConQuest workflow depends on the required model and outputs, not a goal of reproducing every external modeling option.

Step constraints: fixed values and partial sharing

This planned 0.3.x extension would let users fix selected step offsets or share selected transitions across criteria while estimating the remaining steps separately. For example, two criteria could share only the transition from category 0 to 1. Common RSM steps and facet-specific PCM steps already exist; this plan concerns additional constraints, not a new estimation entry.

Priority Planned capability Scope
First Fixed step values and prespecified equalities Extend the existing fit_mfrm() specification, starting with RSM/PCM on one shared category range. Public option names and formats remain to be designed.
Next Reusable constraint groups Simplify repeated declarations of the same supported constraints; first distinguish needs already met by existing step ownership.
Later candidate General linear constraints or design-matrix input Assess separately after the bounded cases work through the supported analysis and reporting routes.

Initial targets are centered step offsets. A location-plus-step threshold has a different meaning and requires separate support. Fixed values and equalities are substantive assumptions; they do not establish category invariance from the data. Constraints must be consistent with centering and an identifiable model. Shared offsets do not permit different category ranges in this scope.

Completion requires consistent estimation, parameter counts, uncertainty, prediction, diagnostics, plots, reports and saved-result reuse. Each estimator, GPCM extension, calibration/export and simulation route needs an explicit support decision; unsupported combinations must fail clearly. Existing defaults and saved fits retain their meanings. This extension is not a prerequisite for maintenance releases or 0.3.0 release.

Current Bayesian export scope and 0.3.x extensions

One-family GPCM MML; JML only with a shared step/slope facet Direct data + spec or mfrm_fit export: estimated intercept-only normal population (stan, with optional run_cmdstan = TRUE) or fixed 𝒩(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) population (stan and brms), with permitted fixed anchors / group means; checksum-bound joint-draw contrasts, arbitrary credible levels, out-of-sample new-Person scoring via predict(), and reporting via read_mfrm_posterior() Connect posterior-predictive rating-plan comparisons where applicable
Two-family GPCM Experimental MML within the named-role scope above Fixed-population Stan export from an explicit mfrm_fit, including additional fixed facets and separate step/location roles; named roles and the prior reference follow posterior reload, contrasts, intervals, plots and reports. Direct data/spec, brms and new-Person posterior scoring remain unsupported Integrate only explicitly supported model extensions; assess interval validity separately from computational support
Person-level latent regression Conditional-normal MML via population_formula Rejected explicitly Bounded 0.3.x extension of export_mfrm_model()
Non-Person facet interactions Supported two-way fixed effects in RSM/PCM via facet_interactions Rejected explicitly Bounded 0.3.x extension of export_mfrm_model()

Covariate interactions inside population_formula and rating-facet interactions in facet_interactions represent different statistical terms with different identification constraints; they will be specified and validated separately rather than merged. Exported Bayesian models share the measurement model’s response equation and add explicit priors; their posterior summaries and credible intervals are not native MML point estimates, Wald intervals, or likelihood-ratio tests. See help("export_mfrm_model"), help("read_mfrm_posterior"), and help("predict.mfrm_posterior_summary").

Plausible values and optional survey-analysis integration

sample_mfrm_plausible_values() already returns approximate Person posterior draws in $values; it remains available in 0.3.0. Supported MML fits use the fitted population, including Person covariates for latent regression. Calibration and population parameters stay fixed. JML-source draws add an explicit scoring prior after calibration; they are not a population distribution estimated by JML. These draws are neither individual true scores nor automatic validation of downstream regressions. See help("sample_mfrm_plausible_values") for model scope, scoring-prior choices, integration checks and saved-result reuse.

mfrmr is responsible for correct scoring, labelled Person/draw values, the calibration and scoring basis, numerical-review information and saved-result reuse. Existing result objects and the plausible_values arguments of export_mfrm_bundle() and build_mfrm_replay_script() provide a general handoff. Improvements to posterior scoring or conditioning require their own measurement justification, independent of a particular survey package.

The PV application shows extraction, inspection and saving, with the conditions for a separate downstream analysis. This does not add a dedicated adapter, dependency or release milestone. A convenience API needs a recurring, generalizable problem that existing outputs cannot reasonably solve. Fixed-calibration draws retain their stated uncertainty limits regardless of which downstream tool is used.

Explanatory models: covariate ownership before more options

Existing Person-level population_formula and person_data support latent regression within their documented MML scope. For one essay or speech per Person, a Person-constant language feature can enter that population model. The fitted total ability and the residual after conditioning are different quantities; the residual is not automatically a fairer score.

Assessment question Existing basis or proposed extension Required distinction
Do vocabulary, syntax or speaking speed relate to performance? Existing Person latent regression for Person-constant features; validate a reproducible applied example One speech cannot separate stable ability from a unique topic or occasion. Feature extraction, missingness and assignment matter.
Does rater experience relate to severity? Candidate 0.3.x extension of the random-rater RSM with a conditional severity mean Experience constant within a rater is confounded with unrestricted fixed rater effects. A conditional random-effect model and a finite-panel secondary contrast answer different questions.
Does a feature matter differently across criteria or performances? Separately specified response-side and within-/between-Person extensions Repeated performances are not independent Persons. Continuous covariate effects, categorical facet interactions and GPCM slopes are distinct terms.

Start a joint extension with a bounded RSM specification and independent probability/likelihood checks, then evaluate realistic assignment and small-rater conditions. PCM, performance-level effects and additional interactions are separate acceptance decisions. Existing TAM/ConQuest design and regression facilities provide comparison routes; mfrmr’s intended contribution is a clear, validated path from model ownership to scores, uncertainty and reports. A general SEM/GLMM engine is outside this plan. These new joint models do not block 0.3.0. See the methodological basis in Mariano & Junker (2007) and the existing ordinal/SEM comparison.

Assessment planning, rater assignment, and feedback principles

G-theory planning and operational design comparison

Univariate and multivariate G-Study and D-Study workflows, paired multivariate D-study comparisons, and design simulations remain first-class capabilities that do not require Bayesian software. Classical observed-score generalizability and IRT/MFRM latent-scale precision answer complementary questions and keep distinct labels, variance denominators, and interval assumptions. Beyond the finite feasible plan comparison in 0.3.0, broader sparse future rosters, adaptive rater allocation, and post-selection plan adjustments remain separate research-backed extensions so single-plan intervals are never overstated as optimal-design guarantees. See help("mfrmr_methods_reference"), help("mfrmr_workflow_methods"), and the vignette("mfrmr-gtheory", package = "mfrmr").

Existing interval choices include scoped F/MLS methods, conservative mean_square_region bounds for balanced designs, and experimental REML profiles. Plan differences can use the documented paired-delta, shared-region or profile routes within their respective scopes. These methods have different assumptions and coverage qualifications; a smaller SE does not establish a more reliable interval. See help("confint.mfrm_multivariate_d_study") and help("mfrm_d_study_comparison") for choosing a supported route.

Improving interval calibration for small rater pools is a separate research question; an MFRM-parameter coverage study cannot answer it.

Rater assignment, linking, and anchors

Guidance and diagnostics for complete and incomplete rating networks distinguish direct parameter anchors, group-mean anchors, and unanchored common-person/common-rater linking. No single percentage of common ratings guarantees a stable common scale across designs: graph connectivity, overlap geometry, anchor fit, and empirical drift all matter. Fixed anchors impose exact scale constraints and do not by themselves establish invariance or propagate prior calibration uncertainty. A scoped direct RSM/PCM MML route can estimate the receiving population mean and variance and add supplied independent-source anchor covariance, using fixed or adaptive integration. This route is intercept-only and excludes groups/interactions. Shared-sample propagation and uncertainty in differences involving the source population mean remain separate from this implemented route. Cohort shifts, panel-wide severity shifts, and individual rater drift require identifiable comparisons; broader support remains a 0.3.x and later task. See the linking and DFF guide and help("mfrm_facet_intervals").

The sample-size stability guide will develop in three stages:

  1. Map the decision and existing evidence. Distinguish Persons, raters, tasks, linking performances and ratings per Person. Name the target: ability, a severity contrast, a cohort difference, population variance or screening accuracy. Descriptive count bands are not adequacy thresholds.
  2. Explore point-estimation sensitivity. Reuse existing studies and vary Person distributions, fixed-facet spread, steps, rater-by-criterion bias, category use and assignment in small, realistic writing/speaking scenarios. Distinguish model misspecification from error under the fitted model; retain failures and numerical-review states. Facet types, level counts and free parameters are different measures of complexity.
  3. Confirm selected recommendations. Evaluate bias/RMSE, interval availability, width and coverage with Monte Carlo uncertainty. For diagnostics, assess false flags and detection; for reliability, name the coefficient and population target. Use independent confirmation for selected design rules, not a universal minimum N derived from a small exploratory study.

The same fits can support these questions where their saved information is sufficient. They cannot turn severity-interval coverage into evidence about Infit detection or G/Phi. Rater separation is not agreement, and increasing ratings cannot remove topic, rubric or recording-mode confounding. Anchor studies must separate source-calibration size, linking information and receiving sample size; bias/DFF studies must distinguish conditional screening from joint interaction estimation and account for multiple comparisons.

Joint RSM/PCM cell and contrast intervals can retain an estimated normal population under direct MML, including adaptive integration and joint information. This removes the need to fix the population solely to obtain those intervals, but does not establish classroom sample-size recommendations.

An explicit experimental method = "profile" in mfrm_facet_intervals() now supports one pairwise contrast in direct RSM/PCM MML with an estimated normal population. It includes zero residual variance in nuisance optimization, uses adaptive integration with refinement checks throughout the profile, and retains both the source and reoptimized estimates. The bounded Task-difference study supports improved availability near the variance boundary, not a universal coverage advantage or minimum sample size. General boundary calibration remains unqualified.

Rater feedback and diagnostic screening

Severity estimates, infit/outfit MnSq and ZSTD, centrality/restriction indices, exact and weighted agreement, bias/DFF screens, residual networks, and exploratory clustering help assessment teams decide which ratings, criteria, or raters warrant substantive review. They are not automatic judgments of test fairness, rater competence, or training causal effects. Future feedback improvements prioritize clearer diagnostic explanations and cohesive mfrm_results() / mfrm_report() synthesis. Evaluate whether intended users can interpret these outputs; working examples and readable figures alone do not establish that outcome.

Matched comparisons include binary MH, explicitly selected multi-category/ multi-group GMH, and cumulative ordinal logistic models for two or more groups. These require independent Persons within each target and justified matching; they do not pool repeated Person-target ratings. GMH supplies an omnibus association test, not a severity estimate. Logistic output separates omnibus group tests from reference/focal point effects on a matching range shared by all groups. Repeated-rating comparisons remain separate development work; finite-sample performance requires evidence beyond numerical convergence.

New screening cutoffs require evidence about false flags and detection under the intended assignment design. The feedback milestone above also requires traceable examples and appropriate review actions.

Public double-scoring data as an applied evaluation candidate

The double-scoring application uses invented observations to explain agreement, missingness and the additional information needed for individual-rater inference. It links to IEA data sources without distributing their records. An agreement analysis and a PV analysis can stand independently. Dataset examples do not create an importer or model milestone; general capabilities are evaluated across relevant rating designs.

Interoperability and computational feasibility

Existing external-software routes provide a baseline; the 0.3.x work is bounded extension of those routes, not the introduction of interoperability:

Software Existing route Candidate change after 0.3.0 Acceptance boundary
FACETS Scorefile/fit-table reading, fit review and terminology guides No new general-equivalence promise; retain explicit convention differences Extreme scores, weights, anchors and fit-statistic degrees of freedom must be compared under matching conventions.
TAM; eRm and mirt Import documented fitted components on the source scale through import_irt_fit() Extend reporting for supported TAM outputs while retaining their source-model meaning DesignCell locations do not identify separate facet effects or their joint covariance without the underlying design mapping. No new generic eRm/mirt importer is planned here.
ConQuest Export bundles and normalization for demonstrated additive overlap specifications Extend comparisons for bounded polytomous additive RSM/PCM specifications Match response equations, scale constraints and uncertainty definitions; retain unsupported cases explicitly.

Do not merge MML, unpenalized JML, bias-corrected JML, CML, G-theory ANOVA/MLS, and Bayesian HMC outputs merely because they produce similarly shaped tables. See the help("mfrmr_gpcm_scope"), help("build_conquest_overlap_bundle"), and help("import_irt_fit").

Sparse-design resource use is part of numerical usability. Current native likelihood paths index observed rating rows and reuse eligible probability calculations; they do not require a complete Person-by-generalized-item response matrix. This is not a fully sparse implementation: quadrature arrays, observed-cell EM workspaces, corrected-JML count tables and joint covariance calculations can still be large. The information-workspace budget is not a cap on total process memory. Priorities are measured peak memory and elapsed time by engine and design, followed by bounded caching, block processing or sparse operators where useful, while preserving likelihoods, gradients, uncertainty checks and failure reasons. First check existing supported paths at matched observed-rating counts while varying Persons, observed cells and imbalance; report integration-node/category counts and free parameters alongside resource use. Generalized-item reshaping for external software is a separate allocation. New covariate/facet extensions must demonstrate feasibility in their declared scope; reducing quadrature accuracy or omitting required inference checks is not a performance improvement.

In 0.3.0, dependent sum-to-zero facet levels remain reportable. Supported MML uncertainty transforms the full free-coordinate covariance to all levels, including covariance terms for the dependent level. Facet fit summaries aggregate observed rows for every level. A dependent level is not a known anchor: fixed values, boundary-related omissions and unavailable information retain separate labels. Ordinary JML’s observation-information SEs remain exploratory and are not the same joint covariance. Free-coordinate coef()/vcov() omit dependent coordinates by design; use mfrm_facet_intervals() and the labelled diagnostic tables for the corresponding all-level results within their supported scopes.

0.4.x and later model branches

New model families will be introduced only when their identification rules, independent numerical reference checks, inferential properties, and practical reporting workflow are established for a concrete assessment question.

Target series Intended capability Initial scope and methodological boundary
0.4.x: Multidimensional rubric profiles Low-dimensional domain profiles, domain correlations, joint profile contrasts, and criterion/rater feedback Start with a prespecified simple between-item binary loading matrix QQ on one rubric facet and unit slopes. Evaluate native MML initially for D∈{2,3}D \in \{2, 3\} and Stan HMC for explicitly supported dimensions, with measured accuracy and resource limits. Verify reduction to the corresponding unit-slope model with matching step, link and scale conventions. Define and validate subscore added value for the intended score before recommending domain reporting.
0.4.x+: Rating-process and response/scoring time models Joint or linked review of rating outcomes with timing observations Model person production/response time and rater scoring time as distinct observation processes; never duplicate one event duration across multiple criterion rows as independent likelihood contributions.
0.4.x+: Direct rater-effect and latent-class extensions Bounded parametric centrality, halo, or restricted rater-class models for targeted operational questions Establish label-switching/scale identification and compare against simpler additive + diagnostic workflows under sparse designs before public adoption.
0.4.x+: Attribute-based cognitive diagnosis Bounded rater-effects cognitive-diagnosis workflow with an explicit discrete skill-QQ matrix Restrict initial support to small, prespecified binary attribute profiles; keep discrete skill-QQ cognitive diagnosis strictly separate in parameterization and interface from continuous multidimensional loading-QQ MFRM and exploratory clustering.
0.4.x+ candidate: Graded response models (GRM) A cumulative-link alternative for a specified ordinal-rating question; not native support in 0.3.0 Define ordered threshold ownership, slope placement and identification; validate category probabilities, derivatives, information, scoring and diagnostics independently. GRM is a different response family from adjacent-category RSM/PCM/GPCM, and does not inherit their CML or bias-correction routes. External cumulative-model comparisons precede a decision to implement.

The initial simple-loading model is not a reproduction of Uto (2021)’s freely varying positive loadings. General cross-loadings require explicit axis and rotation constraints; a prior that selects an orientation is not likelihood identification. Nor does setting one dimension make Uto (2021)’s equation identical to the current Uto & Ueno (2020) type two-family equation. These distinctions must be resolved before implementation or performance studies.

Foundational references for these extensions include Uto & Ueno (2020), Uto (2021), Haberman (2008), Shan & Wang (2020), and Ulitzsch et al. (2023). Haberman’s PRMSE framework motivates the subscore question; its applicability and estimator must be specified for the chosen score target. Better global fit alone does not establish useful subscores. Because these model classes exist in the psychometric literature, mfrmr evaluates contributions by transparency of assumptions, numerical reliability, and end-to-end usability rather than model-name count.

What counts as complete?

Completion is specific to a model, rating design, output and user task:

  1. Correct calculation and scope: equations, scales and constraints are stated; relevant calculations agree with independent references; unsupported inputs are distinguished from numerical failures.
  2. Usable and reproducible results: documented calls, summaries, figures, reports and saved objects agree about the target and its status. Supported older results reload across R sessions, and external-software comparisons retain their model and convention differences.
  3. Appropriate interpretation: numerical checks determine which quantities are available for the dataset. They do not establish model adequacy or finite-sample coverage. A point estimate, its uncertainty and its boundary status may have different qualifications.
  4. Evidence for the claim: a sample-size rule, diagnostic cutoff, optimal plan or comprehension claim needs evidence for that specific use. Interval studies distinguish availability, coverage among available intervals and the fraction of all planned replications returning a covering interval, with failures and Monte Carlo uncertainty retained.

Experimental methods may be offered with explicitly limited evidence. An unresolved general research question does not automatically prevent release of a correct, bounded workflow. Conversely, successful checks or one real-data example cannot establish a general recommendation.

Normal package checks retain representative real calculations and essential regressions; longer research and optional-software checks have their own reproducible execution paths. Final release checks apply to the actual archive. Essential interpretation remains available offline, and website examples must match the documented package version. Publication is complete only when those artifacts are available to users.
